title: Maximum Number of Words Found in Sentences
description:
# Maximum Number of Words Found in Sentences

A **sentence** is a list of one or more words separated by single spaces. There are no leading spaces and no trailing spaces.

You are given an array of strings `sentences`, where each `sentences[i]` is one valid sentence. Return the maximum number of words that appears in any single sentence.

## Example 1:

**Input:** sentences = ["alice and bob love leetcode", "i think so too", "this is great thanks very much"]
**Output:** 6
**Explanation:** The three sentences contain 5, 4, and 6 words. The maximum is 6.

## Example 2:

**Input:** sentences = ["please wait", "continue to fight", "continue to win"]
**Output:** 3
**Explanation:** The second and third sentences both contain 3 words, so the maximum is 3.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= sentences.length <= 100`
* `1 <= sentences[i].length <= 100`
* `sentences[i]` consists only of lowercase English letters and spaces.
* `sentences[i]` does not have leading or trailing spaces.
* All words in `sentences[i]` are separated by a single space.

examples.input: sentences = ["alice and bob love leetcode", "i think so too", "this is great thanks very much"]
sentences = ["please wait", "continue to fight", "continue to win"]

solutions.name: Split Each Sentence
solutions.description:
## Approach

Split each sentence on its single spaces and take the length of the resulting word array. Track the largest length across all sentences.

## Key Insight

This mirrors the problem definition directly: after splitting on spaces, each token is one word because the input guarantees no leading, trailing, or repeated spaces.

## Complexity Analysis

Every character can be scanned while splitting, so the time complexity is O(n*m), where `m` is the maximum sentence length. Each split creates a temporary array for one sentence, so the space complexity is O(m).

solutions.name: Manual Space Count
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each sentence, start the word count at 1 and scan its characters. Every space increases the word count by one.

## Key Insight

The input contract makes spaces reliable separators. Since there are no leading, trailing, or repeated spaces, counting separators is enough and avoids allocating token arrays.

## Complexity Analysis

The scan visits every character once, giving O(n*m) time. Only counters are stored, so the space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: IndexOf Separator Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use `indexOf` to jump from one space separator to the next. Each found separator adds one word, and the search resumes after that separator.

## Key Insight

This keeps the separator-counting model but delegates the inner character search to the standard library. It still uses the rule that words are exactly spaces plus one.

## Complexity Analysis

Across one sentence the search advances through the string, so the total time is O(n*m). The algorithm keeps only a few indexes and counters, so the space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: Length Difference Space Count
solutions.description:
## Approach

Remove spaces from each sentence and compare the original length with the no-space length. The difference is the number of spaces, so the word count is that difference plus one.

## Key Insight

This is another way to count separators without manually iterating over characters in user code. The answer depends on the number of spaces, not on the lengths of the words themselves.

## Complexity Analysis

Replacing spaces scans each sentence, so the time complexity is O(n*m). The no-space string is temporary storage for one sentence, so the space complexity is O(m).
